cues.text: All life on Earth depends on this tiny, energetic molecule: adenosine triphosphate, or ATP.
ATP drives biochemical activity inside your living cells and is a key building block of DNA and RNA.
Generating ATP for your living cells are mitochondria, electrochemical batteries that convert energy from the food you eat and oxygen from the air you breathe into ATP.
So, where does your ATP come from?
Deep inside your mitochondria, rows of molecular motors generate ATP, the molecule essential to all life on Earth.
Enzymes bring together reactants to form a chemical bond, converting mechanical energy into chemical energy.
A ring of enzymes works in step, creating three molecules of ATP with each cycle.
Inside the molecular motor, a rotating axle powers the sequence.
The axle is attached to a rotary molecular motor moved by the force of protons pushing from the other side of the membrane.
A difference in proton concentration propels the molecular mechanism.
Synthesis of ATP.
ATP drives biochemical activity inside your living cells and is a key building block of DNA and RNA.
ATP is the cell's spendable energy. Three phosphates in a row, and the bond to the last one is what gets broken to pay for work.
It pays for almost everything a cell does, and the same molecule minus two phosphates is a letter in DNA and RNA.
Mitochondria make most of it. Food supplies the electrons, oxygen accepts them at the end, and the energy released in between is what this film is about.
The question the animation answers: not what ATP does, but where it is physically assembled.
In the inner mitochondrial membrane, packed with ATP synthase. Each one is a machine, and there are thousands per mitochondrion.
The catalytic head holds ADP and a phosphate close enough, in the right orientation, for the bond to form. Squeezing them together IS the catalysis.
Three catalytic sites around the head, each in a different state at any moment: one binding, one making the bond, one releasing. Three ATP per full turn.
The head does not turn. A central stalk turns inside it, and its asymmetry is what forces each site through the three states in order.
The stalk is driven by a rotor in the membrane. Protons crossing the membrane through the rotor make it spin, the way water turns a wheel.
The gradient is the stored energy. Respiration spends food to pump protons out; they fall back in through this motor, and that fall is what pays for the bond.
Mechanical energy into chemical energy, which is a thing almost no other enzyme does.
You make roughly your own body weight in ATP a day, and hold only a few grams of it at a time. It is spent about as fast as this machine makes it.
